the-principles-of-scientific-management: Frederick Winslow Taylor's 1911 book changed how the world works — literally. Studying factory labor with a stopwatch, he argued that every job could be analyzed, timed, and made more efficient. Factories, offices, and eventually whole economies adopted his methods. Love it or hate it, this short book is the founding text of modern management.
shop-management: Frederick Winslow Taylor's twin to his famous Scientific Management brings his system into the shop and office. Planning rooms, time study, and bonus pay are set forth as plain tools for bosses. Dry but world-changing, the book helped invent the modern art of getting work done.
poems-of-sentiment: Ella Wheeler Wilcox turns to the tender emotions in this companion to her Poems of Purpose — love, sympathy, memory, and hope. Her direct, heartfelt style speaks plainly to the feelings everyone knows. Readers who like their poetry warm and unpretentious will find these verses easy company.
politics-a-treatise-on-government: Aristotle's Politics, set down more than 2,300 years ago, is the first great book on how men are ruled. Looking at law codes, town life, and the best form of the state, the wise Greek asks what makes rule good and towns thrive. All later talk of kings, votes, and tyrants stands in its shade.
army-life-in-a-black-regiment: Thomas Wentworth Higginson commanded the first Black regiment in the Civil War, and this memoir is his tribute to his soldiers. With deep respect he describes their courage, humor, and longing for freedom. A landmark of African American history and one of the finest Civil War memoirs ever written.
picturesque-quebec-a-sequel-to-quebec-pa: Sir James Le Moine, Quebec's devoted historian, leads readers through the old city's gates, shrines, and battlefields. His sequel overflows with lore of the ancient capital. The perfect companion for a walk through North America's most storied town. Battlefields, old gates, and shrines pass in review, told with the love of a lifelong citizen.
the-little-immigrant: Eva Stern tells the story of a little immigrant — a child crossing the ocean to a new land, with all the fear and hope of the journey. Her simple, tender tale speaks for the millions of young newcomers who helped build America. A touching book for young readers.
introduction-to-the-old-testament: John Edgar McFadyen introduces modern readers to the Old Testament — its books, its history, and its meaning. His clear, reverent scholarship guided generations of students. A trusted doorway into the Hebrew scriptures. History, poetry, and prophecy are set forth with clarity and devotion.
the-country-housewife-and-lady-s-directo: Richard Bradley's 18th-century director guides the country housewife through house, dairy, and garden management. Recipes, remedies, and good order fill its practical pages. A delightful window onto Georgian domestic life. Stillrooms, pantries, and herb gardens yield their secrets to her readers.
second-treatise-of-government: John Locke's Second Treatise founded modern liberal thought — life, liberty, and property; government by consent. America's founders drank deep from it. The most influential political essay ever written. Tyrants beware: his words lit the fires of two revolutions. Every schoolboy once knew its arguments by heart.
the-consumer-viewpoint: Mildred Maddocks Bentley examines the consumer viewpoint — what buyers truly need and how markets ought to serve them. Her pioneering home-economics study spoke up for the housewife in an age of new mass selling. An early and thoughtful voice for consumer rights.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abandonment: This 1913 Catholic Encyclopedia article on abandonment — the spiritual act of surrendering oneself to God's will — explains its place in the devout life. John Wynne treats a classic theme of ascetical theology. A thoughtful reference for students of spirituality. The quiet way of trust, set forth with old-school clarity.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-abbey-of-mell: This piece covers Mellifont, Ireland's first Cistercian house. Its lavabo charmed all who saw it. Edmond Obrecht gives its history. The white monks come to Erin. Its monks taught the Irish the new Gothic building ways. Its gatehouse still greets the Drogheda road.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-acanthus-plan: This 1913 reference article on the acanthus — the plant that crowned Corinthian capitals. Thomas Poole traces its art and nature. Callimachus saw beauty in its leaves. A weed that taught architects. Its leaves still curl on bank and courthouse. Gardeners still grow it for its bold leaves.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-accident: This 1913 reference piece on accident in philosophy — what clings to substance without being it. Francis Siegfried explains the scholastic doctrine. Color, size, and place are accidents. The Eucharist gives the doctrine its weight. Aquinas built his Eucharist teaching on the distinction. The schools never let it go.
catholic-encyclopedia-1913-achille-desur: A 1913 entry on Achille Desurmont — the French Redemptorist preacher and writer. John Magnier sketches his zealous life. His missions stirred the faithful. A popular voice of nineteenth-century France. His retreats drew crowds of clergy. Rome made him a consultor of the Index.
